cards.title: Sperling: whole and partial report
cards.aim: How much does sensory (iconic) memory hold, and how long does it last?
cards.manipulated: The report method: whole report (name as many letters as you can), partial report (a tone cues one row right away), and delayed partial report (the tone comes after a delay). The displays were three rows of four letters.
cards.measured: How many letters people could report from a briefly flashed letter array.
cards.found: In whole report people named about a third of the letters. In partial report they named most of the cued row, for any row. In delayed partial report they named only about one letter, and by about one second partial report fell to near the whole-report level.
cards.means: Sensory memory has a large capacity but fast decay; the report limit came from the image fading, not from too little being stored.
cards.trap: Whole report makes capacity look like four or five items, but that is a limit on reporting, not on storage.

cards.title: Brown–Peterson: delay and trial history
cards.aim: How fast does short-term memory fade when rehearsal is blocked?
cards.manipulated: The delay before recall (a few seconds up to about eighteen seconds) and where a trial fell in the series (first trial, third trial, many trials later).
cards.measured: Recall of three letters after counting backward by threes during the delay.
cards.found: On the first trial recall stayed high even after the long delay. On later trials recall after the long delay dropped, and after many trials it fell to almost nothing. Averaged over all trials, recall fell with delay.
cards.means: Forgetting in short-term memory comes from proactive interference as well as decay; earlier trigrams made the new one harder to keep.
cards.trap: The average curve looks like pure decay over time, but it hides that the big drops came from later trials.

cards.title: Visual change detection and complexity
cards.aim: Is visual short-term memory capacity set by the number of items or by the amount of information in them?
cards.manipulated: Set size (number of colored squares), what changed in colored bars (angle, color, or both), and object complexity (colored squares, Chinese characters, random polygons, shaded cubes).
cards.measured: Whether people judged a second display (S2) the same as or different from a briefly flashed first display (S1).
cards.found: Accuracy fell dramatically above about four items. Remembering two features of a bar was about as easy as one. Capacity fell as objects got more complex, from about four for colored squares to fewer than two for shaded cubes.
cards.means: Visual short-term memory holds about three to four whole objects, and capacity depends on how much information each object carries.
cards.trap: Do not say the limit is always seven items; for visual memory the slides give about four, and fewer for complex objects.

cards.title: Digit-span training and chess expertise
cards.researcher: Ericsson and colleagues; Chase and Simon
cards.aim: Can chunking and knowledge let people hold much more in short-term memory?
cards.manipulated: For Ericsson: training a college student on digit span. For Chase and Simon: player skill (masters vs beginners) and board type (real-game arrangement vs random arrangement).
cards.measured: Digit span for the trained student; number of chess pieces placed correctly after a brief look at a board.
cards.found: The trained student's digit span rose to around eighty digits by chunking digits into running times. Masters placed far more pieces than beginners on real-game boards but were no better on random boards.
cards.means: Chunking with knowledge from long-term memory stretches capacity; experts do not have bigger short-term memories.
cards.trap: The masters' advantage disappears with random boards, so it is knowledge of real patterns, not a larger store.

cards.title: Conrad · sound-based errors after visual presentation
cards.aim: When letters are seen, are errors based on how they look or how they sound?
cards.manipulated: Whether the flashed letters were similar or not similar (half of the presentations each).
cards.measured: Writing down the letters after a brief visual flash.
cards.found: Errors more often swapped in a letter that sounded like the target (E replaced by B) than one that looked like it (F for E).
cards.means: Seen letters are recoded into a sound-based form in working memory (phonological similarity effect).
cards.trap: The letters came in through vision, but the confusions followed sound; presentation format is not the same as memory code.

cards.title: Word length, bilingual digit span, and articulatory suppression
cards.researcher: Baddeley and colleagues (1975, 1984); Ellis and Hennelly (1980)
cards.aim: What limits how much verbal material the phonological loop can hold?
cards.manipulated: Word length (short vs long words), language of the digits (Welsh vs English for bilingual children), and speaking while memorizing (articulatory suppression).
cards.measured: Memory for word lists and digit span.
cards.found: People remembered more short words than long words. Welsh-English bilingual children had a shorter digit span in Welsh because Welsh number names take longer to say. Suppression lowered recall and reduced both the word-length and phonological similarity effects.
cards.means: Verbal span depends on how much can be rehearsed in about 1.5 to 2 seconds, and speech-based rehearsal is used to maintain verbal information.
cards.trap: The Welsh-English gap comes from pronunciation time, not from the numbers' values.

cards.title: Brooks · sentence and F dual-task comparisons
cards.aim: Does a response interfere more when it uses the same kind of memory as the thing being held?
cards.manipulated: Response mode: speaking vs pointing, for two memory tasks (a memorized sentence with noun judgments, and a memorized F with inside/outside corner judgments).
cards.measured: How easy each task was under each response mode.
cards.found: With the sentence, pointing was easier than speaking. With the F, speaking was easier than pointing.
cards.means: Interference depends on the combination of tasks, which supports some independence between verbal and visual or spatial memory.
cards.trap: The results reverse across the two tasks, so neither speaking nor pointing is easier overall.

cards.title: Shepard and Metzler · angle and mental-rotation time
cards.aim: Do people mentally rotate objects, and does more rotation take more time?
cards.manipulated: The angle of rotation between pairs of block-built objects (picture-plane and depth rotation).
cards.measured: Reaction time to judge whether the two objects matched.
cards.found: For picture-plane pairs, reaction time increased as the angle increased, approximately linearly.
cards.means: Larger angles need a larger mental transformation, consistent with an active operation on a spatial representation.
cards.trap: Picture-plane rotation turns within the flat plane; depth rotation turns in three-dimensional space.

cards.title: Vogel · relevant load, distractors, and filtering efficiency
cards.aim: Do people with higher working-memory capacity keep irrelevant items out better?
cards.manipulated: Capacity group (higher vs lower) and display type: two relevant red bars, four relevant red bars, or two red bars plus two irrelevant blue bars.
cards.measured: A memory-related ERP response during the 900 ms retention interval, plus a change judgment on the relevant orientations.
cards.found: High-capacity people showed a larger response for four items than two, and little change when blue distractors were added. For low-capacity people, adding distractors raised the response toward the four-item level. Capacity correlated positively with filtering efficiency.
cards.means: Capacity depends on which items get in as well as how many targets there are; better filtering goes with higher capacity.
cards.trap: A bigger response means a stronger negative deflection, not a more positive voltage.

cards.title: Köhler · circle representation and equal diagonals
cards.aim: Can reorganizing how a problem is represented make a hidden relationship usable?
cards.manipulated: Not a comparison of groups; it is a demonstration of how representing the circle problem as a rectangle changes the solution.
cards.measured: Finding the length of line x when the circle's radius is r.
cards.found: Seeing the black line as a diagonal of a rectangle makes it equal to the dashed radius (the other diagonal), so x = r.
cards.means: Restructuring the representation, not new calculation, makes the answer available.
cards.trap: Do not treat x as an isolated unknown inside the circle; the key is spotting the rectangle with equal diagonals.

cards.title: Metcalfe and Wiebe · insight puzzles and warmth judgments
cards.aim: Do people feel gradually closer to a solution for insight problems as they do for noninsight problems?
cards.manipulated: Problem type: insight problems (triangle and chain) vs noninsight problems (algebra).
cards.measured: Warmth ratings (hot means close to the solution) given every 15 seconds while solving.
cards.found: For algebra, warmth rose gradually as the solution approached. For insight problems, warmth stayed low until close to the solution and then jumped sharply, from about 3 to 7.
cards.means: Insight solutions come with a sudden change in felt progress, unlike methodical noninsight solving.
cards.trap: Not all problem solving is sudden; the sudden jump describes insight problems, not algebra.

cards.title: Candle problem · matchbox presentation and functional fixedness
cards.aim: Does seeing an object only in its familiar use block its use for something else?
cards.manipulated: Whether the matches were inside the box or the matchboxes were empty.
cards.measured: Whether participants solved the problem of mounting the candle on a vertical corkboard so it burns without dripping wax on the floor.
cards.found: Participants given empty matchboxes were twice as likely to solve the problem.
cards.means: Functional fixedness: treating the box only as a container hides its use as a platform for the candle.
cards.trap: The materials were enough to solve it; the obstacle was the familiar use of the box.

cards.title: Two-string problem · pliers as a weight and a movement hint
cards.aim: What helps people see a new use for an object in the two-string problem?
cards.manipulated: Whether an experimenter 'accidentally' set a string in motion (the hint).
cards.measured: Whether participants solved the problem of tying together two strings hanging too far apart to reach.
cards.found: After the swinging hint, most participants were able to solve the problem. The solution is to tie the pliers on a string as a weight and make it swing like a pendulum.
cards.means: The hint helped restructure the representation, so the string became something that can be swung within reach.
cards.trap: The pliers' useful property is their weight, not their ability to grip; that is the functional fixedness.

cards.title: Water-jug problems · practice and a simpler available solution
cards.aim: Can a method that worked earlier block a simpler solution?
cards.manipulated: Practice with the early problems that Practice with early problems solved by B − A − 2C, then new problems (7 and 8) with capacities where a simpler solution exists.
cards.measured: Not measured with participants on the slide; it traces which solution method each problem allows.
cards.found: Repeated success with B − A − 2C builds a mental set. In problem 7 the goal 18 can be reached by A + C, and in problem 8 the goal 25 by A − C, but the familiar method still works and is brought first.
cards.means: A mental set can inhibit a simpler solution even when the familiar one remains possible.
cards.trap: The familiar method still works in problems 7 and 8; the set blocks the simpler one, not the correct answer.

cards.title: Search demonstrations · tile puzzle and Tower of Hanoi subgoals
cards.aim: How can solving be described as search through a problem space using operators and subgoals?
cards.manipulated: Nothing varied; these are worked demonstrations with the Tower of Hanoi and a numbered-tile puzzle.
cards.measured: Not measured with participants; the slides trace states, legal moves, and subgoals.
cards.found: Operators set which moves are legal; routes pass through intermediate states; a search tree shows branches of alternative states. In the Tower of Hanoi, subgoals free the large disk, free the third peg, then move the large disk.
cards.means: Means–end analysis reduces the difference between the current state and the goal by achieving subgoals.
cards.trap: A subgoal is an intermediate condition that makes a move possible, not the final answer.

cards.title: Mutilated checkerboard · labels, pairing, and think-aloud protocols
cards.aim: Does how a problem is stated change how hard it is to find the pairing constraint?
cards.manipulated: Information on the board: blank, colored, labeled black and pink, or labeled bread and butter.
cards.measured: How fast participants solved the covering problem, along with think-aloud reports of their thoughts.
cards.found: Participants solved the bread-and-butter condition twice as fast as the blank condition. Think-aloud reports showed a shift from squares as positions to the relation between the two kinds of square.
cards.means: Labels pointing to the right representation (one of each kind per domino) reduce solving time, matching Gestalt restructuring.
cards.trap: Equal total area (62 squares, 31 dominoes) does not mean a covering is possible; the colors are unequal.

contrasts.title: Whole report vs partial report

a.definition: The person names as many letters as possible from the flashed array.

b.definition: A tone cues one row to report, so only that row is named.

contrasts.tell: Whole report gave about a third of the letters, partial report gave most of the cued row. The gap shows that more was stored than people could report.
contrasts.example: Sperling's three rows of four letters: the top row was cued by a tone.

contrasts.title: Maintenance rehearsal vs elaborative rehearsal

a.definition: Repeating information silently so it stays in short-term memory longer.

b.definition: Linking new information to knowledge already in long-term memory.

contrasts.tell: Maintenance only keeps information alive while the repeating continues. Elaborative adds meaning and helps move information into long-term memory.
contrasts.example: Saying a phone number over and over is maintenance; connecting it to something you already know is elaborative.

contrasts.title: Retroactive vs proactive interference

a.definition: A new memory interferes with remembering old information.

b.definition: An old memory interferes with remembering new information.

contrasts.tell: Ask which memory is doing the interfering. New hurting old is retroactive; old hurting new is proactive.
contrasts.example: A new phone number crowding out the old one is retroactive; earlier trigrams harming the current one in Brown-Peterson is proactive.

contrasts.title: Decay vs interference

a.definition: A memory trace vanishes simply because time passes.

b.definition: Forgetting caused by one memory competing with or replacing another.

contrasts.tell: Decay depends on time alone; interference depends on what else is in memory. Brown and Peterson and Peterson meant to test decay but found interference as well.
contrasts.example: Recall after the long delay was fine on the first trial but near zero many trials later.

contrasts.title: Icon vs echo

a.definition: A fleeting mental image; the visual form of sensory memory.

b.definition: The brief continuation of a sound in the auditory system.

contrasts.tell: Icon is for seeing and echo is for hearing; both are sensory memory lasting under a second.
contrasts.example: Sperling studied iconic memory; replaying the last few words someone said is an echo.

contrasts.title: Episodic vs semantic memory

a.definition: Memory for personal events we lived through.

b.definition: Memory for facts and general knowledge.

contrasts.tell: Episodic ties to a particular time and place; semantic is general knowledge.
contrasts.example: Remembering one particular birthday is episodic; knowing what a birthday is is semantic.

contrasts.title: Phonological loop vs visuospatial sketchpad

a.definition: Maintains verbal and auditory information, with a phonological store and articulatory rehearsal.

b.definition: Holds visual and spatial information such as appearance and arrangement.

contrasts.tell: Ask whether the content is sounds and words or shapes and locations. Brooks's reversed results show they are partly separate.
contrasts.example: A remembered sentence uses the loop; the remembered F uses the sketchpad.

contrasts.title: Word-length effect vs phonological similarity effect

a.definition: Lists of short words are remembered better than lists of long words.

b.definition: Items that sound alike are confused.

contrasts.tell: Word length is about rehearsal time; similarity is about overlapping sounds. Articulatory suppression reduces both.
contrasts.example: Welsh digits take longer to say, so span is shorter; E is confused with B because they sound alike.

contrasts.title: Functional fixedness vs mental set

a.definition: Restricting an object to its familiar functions.

b.definition: A preconceived notion about how to approach a problem, based on past experience with that problem or similar problems.

contrasts.tell: Fixedness is about an object's use; a set is about a method of solving.
contrasts.example: Seeing the matchbox only as a container is fixedness; repeating B − A − 2C in the water-jug problems is a set.

contrasts.title: Insight vs noninsight problems

a.definition: Solved by a sudden realization after restructuring, as in the triangle and chain problems.

b.definition: Solved by successive operations that bring the solver closer, as in algebra.

contrasts.tell: Look at warmth: it rises gradually for noninsight problems but jumps late, from about 3 to 7, for insight problems.
contrasts.example: Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) compared the triangle and chain problems with algebra.

questions: Which stage of the modal model holds about five to seven items for roughly fifteen to twenty seconds?
What is the difference between maintenance rehearsal and elaborative rehearsal?
Why is rehearsal called a control process?
What is the role of attention between sensory memory and short-term memory?
Which concept is this an example of: placing items along an imagined building to make them memorable?
ask.remember: The modal model runs sensory, then short-term, then long-term memory; attention gets items into short-term memory, and rehearsal and other control processes are chosen by the person.

questions: What did Sperling find about whole report compared with partial report?
What was manipulated in Sperling's experiment?
Why did delayed partial report produce only about one letter?
What did people believe about iconic memory before Sperling, and why was it wrong?
How does an icon differ from an echo?
ask.remember: Sensory memory has large capacity but fast decay; whole report underestimates it because the image fades while reporting.

questions: Why did Brown and Peterson and Peterson have participants count backward by threes?
What happened to recall after a long delay on the first trial versus many trials later?
Which concept is this an example of: earlier trigrams making new letters harder to recall?
How does retroactive interference differ from proactive interference?
Why does the average over all trials give a misleading impression?
ask.remember: Counting blocks rehearsal; the trial-by-trial pattern shows proactive interference, so forgetting is both decay and interference.

questions: What did Miller propose about short-term memory capacity?
What did Alvarez and Cavanagh find as object complexity increased?
What was manipulated in Chase and Simon's chess study, and what was found?
What did Ericsson's trained student do to reach a digit span of around eighty?
How does chunking increase capacity without enlarging the store?
ask.remember: Capacity is about units, not raw items: visual memory holds about three to four objects, fewer if complex, and chunking uses long-term knowledge to pack more into each slot.

questions: What did Baddeley and Hitch (1974) propose?
What does the central executive do, compared with the phonological loop?
Why does mental multiplication of 43 times 6 need both storage and processing?
What component did Baddeley add in 2000?
How does the working-memory model differ from Atkinson and Shiffrin's short-term memory?
ask.remember: Working memory stores and manipulates information using a central executive, phonological loop, and visuospatial sketchpad, with the episodic buffer added later.

questions: What did Conrad (1964) find about errors with seen letters?
What was manipulated in Conrad's study?
What is the word-length effect, and who found it?
Why did Welsh-English bilingual children have a shorter digit span in Welsh (Ellis and Hennelly, 1980)?
What does articulatory suppression do to the word-length and phonological similarity effects?
ask.remember: Seen letters are recoded into sound, and verbal span depends on rehearsal time; speaking while memorizing disrupts the loop.

ask.topic: Spatial representations and Brooks’s response reversal
questions: What did Brooks (1968) find about the sentence task and the F task?
What was manipulated in Brooks's experiments?
Why was pointing easier for the sentence but speaking easier for the F?
What does the reversal suggest about verbal and visuospatial memory?
Which component is used when holding the shape of an F in mind?
ask.remember: A response is harder when it uses the same kind of memory as the task: sentence with speaking, F with pointing.

questions: What did Shepard and Metzler (1971) find about angle and reaction time?
What is the difference between picture-plane and depth rotation?
What are Miyake and colleagues' (2000) updating, shifting, and inhibition?
Why is the central executive sometimes criticized as a homunculus?
Which concept is this an example of: suppressing irrelevant information to keep the current goal?
ask.remember: Reaction time rises with rotation angle, and the central executive controls attention through updating, shifting, and inhibition.

ask.topic: Integrated episodes and filtering individual differences
questions: What does the episodic buffer do and what is its capacity?
What did Vogel and colleagues (2005) find for high-capacity versus low-capacity participants when distractors were added?
What was manipulated in Vogel's task?
How is filtering efficiency related to working-memory capacity?
Why can some amnesic patients immediately recall a just-heard story?
ask.remember: The buffer binds loop, sketchpad, and long-term information into episodes; higher capacity goes with better filtering of distractors.

questions: What are the present state, goal, and obstacle in a problem?
What did Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) find about warmth ratings for algebra versus insight problems?
What was manipulated in Metcalfe and Wiebe's study?
What is restructuring, and how does it solve Köhler's circle problem?
How does the triangle problem or chain problem require a change in representation?
ask.remember: A problem has a present state, goal, and obstacle; insight follows restructuring and feels sudden, unlike gradual algebra.

ask.topic: Fixation, functional fixedness, and mental set
questions: What did the empty matchbox condition change in the candle problem?
What is functional fixedness, and how does it apply to the pliers in the two-string problem?
What is a mental set, and how does the water-jug procedure B − A − 2C illustrate it?
Which concept is this an example of: failing to see a simpler solution because a familiar method worked before?
How does fixation differ from a mental set?
ask.remember: Functional fixedness is about an object's familiar use; mental set is about a familiar method. Both hide a workable solution.

ask.topic: Problem spaces, operators, and means–end analysis
questions: What are the initial state, intermediate states, and goal state in a problem space?
What do operators do in the Tower of Hanoi?
What is a subgoal, and what are the Tower of Hanoi subgoals?
What does means–end analysis try to reduce?
What does a search tree show for the tile puzzle?
ask.remember: Newell and Simon describe solving as search through states using operators; means–end analysis reduces the gap to the goal by achieving subgoals.

questions: Why can 31 dominoes not cover the mutilated checkerboard?
What conditions were compared in the checkerboard experiment, and what was found?
How did the bread-and-butter labels help solvers?
What is a think-aloud protocol, and what does it reveal?
Which concept is this an example of: a change in representation that makes a constraint available?
ask.remember: Opposite corners are the same color, so colors are unequal; labels like bread and butter made the pairing constraint easier to see, and solving was twice as fast as blank.

explainers.title: Mental multiplication: 43 times 6
explainers.plain: This shows storage and processing working together: you hold one number while you work on another.
steps: Hold the 8 in memory and carry the 1 over the 4.
6 x 4 = 24, then add the carried 1 to get 25.
Combine the 25 with the held 8 to get 258.
explainers.example: Holding the 8 is storage; carrying the 1 and doing the next multiplication and addition is processing.
explainers.watchOut: Do not say working memory only holds numbers; the 8 must survive while other operations are done.

explainers.title: Tower of Hanoi with subgoals
explainers.plain: You cannot move the big disk until it is free and the target peg is free, so you set up those conditions first.
steps: Goal: move the large disk to the third peg.
Subgoal 1: free the large disk by moving the smallest disk to the third peg and the next disk to the middle peg.
Subgoal 2: free the third peg by moving the smallest disk from the third peg onto the smaller stack on the middle peg.
Subgoal 3: move the largest disk from the starting peg to the third peg.
Then move the smaller disks onto it, never putting a larger disk on a smaller one.
explainers.example: The slide's example: the smallest disk goes to the third peg, the next disk to the middle peg, then the smallest goes onto the middle stack.
explainers.watchOut: Achieving a subgoal is not the finished puzzle; the smaller disks still have to reach the third peg.

explainers.title: Mutilated checkerboard
explainers.plain: Each domino covers one square of each color, so the board must have equal numbers of the two colors.
steps: A full board has 64 squares and takes 32 dominoes.
Remove two opposite corners and 62 squares remain, matching 31 dominoes in area.
Every domino covers one square of each color.
Opposite corners are the same color, so one color now has fewer squares.
Equal numbers are needed, so no covering is possible.
explainers.example: The bread-and-butter labels make it clear that each domino needs one bread and one butter.
explainers.watchOut: Equal area (62 squares, 31 dominoes) does not guarantee a legal covering.

explainers.title: Chain problem
explainers.plain: Treat a whole section of chain as the source of connectors instead of opening one link at a time.
steps: Opening a link costs 2 cents and closing it costs 3 cents, so opening and closing one link costs 5 cents.
The budget is 15 cents, so you can open and close three links.
Open the three links of one three-link section.
Use each opened link to join the other three sections into a closed loop, closing each once.
explainers.example: Four short sections become one closed loop for exactly 15 cents.
explainers.watchOut: Opening and closing one link costs 5 cents, so 15 cents allows only three links; use one whole section as the connectors.

explainers.title: Triangle problem
explainers.plain: Move three dots from a ten-dot upward triangle so it points down, keeping seven in place.
steps: Start with ten dots in four rows, with the point on top.
Move the original top dot to a new bottom point beneath the center of the original bottom row.
Move the two outer dots of the original bottom row to the outer ends of the original two-dot row.
That row now has four dots, with three, two, and one below it.
explainers.example: Only three dots move and seven stay put, giving a downward-pointing triangle.

explainers.title: Water-jug problems and mental set
explainers.plain: A rule that worked on early problems can stop you seeing a shorter route later.
steps: Early problems use B − A − 2C, for example 127 − 21 − 3 − 3 = 100.
Problem 7 (A 15, B 39, C 3, goal 18): the familiar way is 39 − 15 − 6 = 18, but A + C gives 18 directly.
Problem 8 (A 28, B 59, C 3, goal 25): A − C gives 25 directly, although B − A − 2C also works.
explainers.example: Problem 8: 28 − 3 = 25 is simpler than the familiar method.
explainers.watchOut: The familiar method still works in problems 7 and 8; the issue is that it blocks the simpler one.

notes: Slide 6:44 notes that the shapes labeled Chinese characters are really parts of characters and one is drawn incorrectly; the slide says this does not change the result.

Slide 10:14 says the 64-disk Tower of Hanoi would take roughly a trillion years at one move per second; the exact minimum (2^64 - 1 moves) works out to roughly 585 billion years, so 'roughly a trillion' is a rounded figure.

Slide 6:38 says the limit of about seven may apply to verbal lists while visual memory holds fewer (about three to four); accepted science also now often cites about four items for working memory generally, so be careful which number the question asks about.

Slide 6:25 and 6:28 describe Brown-Peterson as showing proactive interference as well as decay; some accounts still treat the original decay interpretation as supported, but the slides stress interference.
The Candle, two-string, and water-jug slides name no researcher, so no researcher is given on those cards.
Sperling, Brown and Peterson and Peterson, Alvarez and Cavanagh, Köhler, and Newell and Simon (on pages 13-18) appear without a year on the experiment slides, so none is given on the cards.
